title: Officina Volcani. Euandri consilium
titleEn: Vulcan's Forge and Evander's Offer — Aeneid VIII.407–519
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: At midnight, at the hour when a poor woman who lives by her spinning gets up to rake the embers and set her maids to work, so that she can keep her marriage honest and bring up her children, Vulcan rises from his wife's soft bed and goes to his workshop. It lies under a smoking island beside Lipari, off the coast of Sicily, where the Cyclopes' anvils boom in the caverns and the iron hisses in the furnaces. There the Cyclopes, Brontes, Steropes and Pyragmon, are busy with three jobs at once: a thunderbolt for Jupiter, half finished, built up out of rays of hail, rain-cloud, fire and wind; a chariot for Mars; and the aegis of Pallas Athena, with its snakes and the Gorgon's severed head. Vulcan tells them to drop everything: arms are wanted for a fighting man. They share out the work, and the bronze and gold flow and the steel melts as they shape a huge shield of seven layers, working the bellows, quenching the hissing metal and swinging their hammers in time. Virgil is rewriting the scene in Iliad 18 where Hephaestus forges new armour for Achilles. Meanwhile, at dawn, in Pallanteum, the birds wake old Evander, who dresses, straps on his sword and comes out with his two watchdogs to find Aeneas. In private he tells him the news. His own strength is small, but there is help at hand: the Etruscans of Agylla have thrown out their king, Mezentius, a tyrant who used to kill men by tying them face to face with corpses, and he has taken refuge with Turnus. All Etruria is up in arms to get him back for punishment, but a soothsayer has told them that no Italian may lead them, and their leader Tarchon has offered the command to Evander, who is too old for it. Evander's own son is half Sabine and so ruled out. Aeneas, a foreigner whom the fates call, must take the command, and Evander will send Pallas with him, with two hundred Arcadian horsemen, to learn the work of war under him.

sentences.t:
Inde ubi prima quies medio iam noctis abactae
curriculo expulerat somnum, cum femina primum,
cui tolerare colo vitam tenuique Minerva
impositum, cinerem et sopitos suscitat ignes,
sentences.l:
Then, when first rest, in the middle now of the night driven on
its course, had driven out sleep, at the time a woman first,
on whom to sustain by the distaff her life and by slender Minerva
it is laid, the ash and the slumbering rouses fires,
sentences.i: Then, when the first rest of the night had driven sleep away, with night's chariot now half-way along its course, at the hour when a woman whose lot it is to keep herself alive by her distaff and the fine work of Minerva first wakes the ashes and the sleeping fire,
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. A comma-ended unit: the sentence runs to 415. 'prima quies… expulerat somnum', 'first rest had driven out sleep': the first sleep of the night is over; 'quies' is two syllables, qui-ēs. 'medio… curriculo', 'in the middle of its course', ablative of time, with 'noctis abactae', 'of the night driven on', pictured as a chariot: 'at midnight'. 'cum femina primum… suscitat', 'when a woman first rouses'. 'cui… impositum (est)', 'on whom it is laid', impersonal, with 'tolerare… vitam', 'to sustain her life'. 'colo… tenuique Minerva', 'by the distaff and slender Minerva', the goddess standing for the craft of spinning. 'cinerem et sopitos… ignes', the embers banked overnight. Homer has a simile of an honest working woman weighing out wool to earn a meagre wage for her children (Iliad 12, from memory). Elisions 'Ind(e) ubi', 'ciner(em) et'.

sentences.t:
noctem addens operi, famulasque ad lumina longo
exercet penso, castum ut servare cubile
coniugis et possit parvos educere natos:
sentences.l:
adding the night to the work, and her maids by the lamps at a long
keeps busy task, so that chaste she may keep the bed
of her husband and may be able her little to rear sons:
sentences.i: adding the night to her day's work, and keeps her maids toiling by lamplight at a long stint of spinning, so that she can keep her husband's bed chaste and bring up her little children:
sentences.n: 'noctem addens operi', 'adding the night to her work', 'operi' dative with 'addens'. 'famulas… exercet', 'keeps her maids at work'. 'ad lumina', 'by the lamps'. 'longo… penso', 'at a long task', framing 'exercet'; 'pensum' (from 'pendo', 'weigh') is the weight of wool weighed out to a spinner as her day's work. 'ut… possit', purpose, with two infinitives: 'castum… servare cubile coniugis', 'to keep her husband's bed chaste', i.e. to live honestly without having to sell herself, and 'parvos educere natos', 'to rear her small children'. 'castum… cubile', framing 'ut servare'. 'coniugis' is 'con-iu-gis', the i a consonant. The colon closes the simile; the comparison comes next. Elisions 'noct(em) addens', 'famulasqu(e) ad', 'cast(um) ut'.

sentences.t:
haud secus Ignipotens nec tempore segnior illo
mollibus e stratis opera ad fabrilia surgit.
sentences.l:
not otherwise the Fire-lord, nor at that time more sluggish,
from soft coverlets to his works of the smithy rises.
sentences.i: just so the Lord of Fire, and no more slothful at that hour, rose from his soft bed to the labours of his forge.
sentences.n: 'haud secus', 'not otherwise', 'just so', the second half of the simile. 'Ignipotens', 'mighty in fire', Vulcan's title, used as a name. 'nec… segnior', 'no more sluggish', litotes: as early and as eager as the poor woman. 'tempore… illo', 'at that time', ablative of time. 'mollibus e stratis', 'from his soft coverlets', the bed where Venus has just won him over (8.405–406): the god leaves his wife's embrace to work for her son, the woman works to keep her marriage chaste, and the contrast is pointed. 'opera ad fabrilia', 'to his smith's work', 'fabrilis' from 'faber', 'smith'. 'surgit', present, vivid. Elision 'oper(a) ad'.

sentences.t:
Insula Sicanium iuxta latus Aeoliamque
erigitur Liparen, fumantibus ardua saxis,
sentences.l:
An island beside the Sicanian flank and Aeolian
rises up, Lipare, steep with smoking rocks,
sentences.i: Beside the coast of Sicily and Aeolian Lipare an island rises, sheer, with its smoking rocks,
sentences.n: A comma-ended unit: the sentence runs to 422 and is split at its comma. 'Insula… erigitur', 'an island rises up'. 'iuxta', 'beside', governs both 'Sicanium… latus', 'the Sicanian side', the flank of Sicily ('Sicani', an old people of the island), and 'Aeoliam… Liparen', 'Aeolian Lipare', 'Liparen' the Greek accusative of 'Lipare', the chief of the Aeolian islands, the home of Aeolus and his winds (1.52). The island meant is the one the ancients called Hiera and Vulcania, today Vulcano, beside Lipari. 'fumantibus… saxis', 'with smoking rocks', ablative of respect with 'ardua', 'steep'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
quam subter specus et Cyclopum exesa caminis
antra Aetnaea tonant validique incudibus ictus
auditi referunt gemitus striduntque cavernis
stricturae Chalybum et fornacibus ignis anhelat,
Volcani domus et Volcania nomine tellus.
sentences.l:
under which a cave and, by the Cyclopes eaten out with forges,
caverns Aetnaean thunder, and on the anvils mighty blows,
heard, give back groans, and hiss in the hollows
the ingots of the Chalybes, and in the furnaces the fire pants:
Vulcan's home and Vulcanian by name the land.
sentences.i: and beneath it a cave and caverns hollowed out by the Cyclopes' forges, like Etna's own, thunder, and the heavy blows of hammers on anvils are heard and echo with a groan, the bars of Chalybean iron hiss in the hollows, and fire pants in the furnaces: it is Vulcan's home, and the land is called Vulcania after him.
sentences.n: 'quam subter', 'beneath which', the preposition after its relative (anastrophe). 'specus et… antra… tonant', 'a cave and caverns thunder'. 'Cyclopum exesa caminis', 'eaten out by the Cyclopes' forges', 'Cyclopum… caminis' enclosing 'exesa': the furnaces have hollowed the rock. 'Aetnaea', 'Aetnaean': the Cyclopes' smithy is more usually put under Etna. 'validi… ictus', 'mighty blows', 'incudibus', 'on the anvils', 'auditi', 'heard', 'referunt gemitus', 'return groans', echo. 'stricturae Chalybum', 'the ingots of the Chalybes', masses of wrought iron; the Chalybes, a people on the Black Sea, were famous ironworkers, and their name gives the Latin 'chalybs', 'steel' (446). 'ignis anhelat', 'the fire pants'. 'Volcani domus', in apposition to 'insula'; 'Volcania nomine tellus', 'a land Vulcanian by name'. Elisions 'Cyclop(um) exesa', 'antr(a) Aetnaea', 'validiqu(e) incudibus', 'Chalyb(um) et'.

sentences.t: Hoc tunc ignipotens caelo descendit ab alto.
sentences.l: Hither then the fire-lord from high heaven descends.
sentences.i: To this place the Lord of Fire now came down from high heaven.
sentences.n: 'Hoc', an old form of 'huc', 'hither', not the pronoun. 'ignipotens' is printed here with a small letter, at 414 with a capital; the word is the same title, and the print is kept. 'caelo… ab alto', 'from high heaven', framing 'descendit', the preposition between adjective and noun. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ferrum exercebant vasto Cyclopes in antro,
Brontesque Steropesque et nudus membra Pyragmon.
sentences.l:
Iron were working, in a vast cave, the Cyclopes,
both Brontes and Steropes and, naked as to his limbs, Pyragmon.
sentences.i: In the vast cave the Cyclopes were working iron, Brontes and Steropes and Pyragmon, his limbs bare.
sentences.n: 'Ferrum exercebant', 'they were working iron', the imperfect of work in progress when the god arrives. 'vasto… in antro', framing 'Cyclopes'. The names are Greek and speak for themselves: Brontes 'Thunderer', Steropes 'Lightning-man', Pyragmon 'Fire-anvil'. Hesiod names the three Cyclopes who made Zeus's thunderbolt Brontes, Steropes and Arges (Theogony, from memory); Virgil's third, Pyragmon, takes the place of Arges. 'Brontesque Steropesque', the double '-que', the first '-que' scanned long before 'St-'. 'nudus membra', 'naked as to his limbs', the Greek accusative of respect. Elisions 'Ferr(um) exercebant', 'Steropesqu(e) et'.

sentences.t:
His informatum manibus iam parte polita
fulmen erat, toto genitor quae plurima caelo
deicit in terras, pars inperfecta manebat.
sentences.l:
By these shaped by hands, now a part polished,
a thunderbolt was, of those which from all the sky the father very many
hurls down on the lands; a part unfinished remained.
sentences.i: Their hands had shaped a thunderbolt, of the kind the Father hurls down in such numbers from every quarter of the sky upon the earth; part of it was already polished, part remained unfinished.
sentences.n: 'His informatum manibus… fulmen erat', 'a thunderbolt had been shaped by these men's hands', 'informatum… erat' the pluperfect passive, split across the line. 'parte polita', ablative absolute, 'a part having been polished', answered by 'pars inperfecta manebat', 'part remained unfinished'. 'quae plurima', 'of those which… in great numbers': the relative is plural after the singular 'fulmen', thinking of thunderbolts in general. 'toto… caelo', 'from the whole sky', framing 'genitor quae plurima', 'genitor', 'the father', Jupiter. 'deicit', 'throws down', three syllables, dē-i-cit. 'inperfecta' is Greenough's spelling of 'imperfecta', the prefix not assimilated. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Tris imbris torti radios, tris nubis aquosae
addiderant, rutili tris ignis et alitis austri:
sentences.l:
Three of twisted rain rays, three of cloud watery
they had added, of ruddy three fire and of winged south wind:
sentences.i: They had added three rays of hail and three of rain-cloud, three of red fire and three of the winged south wind:
sentences.n: The making of the thunderbolt, piece by piece. 'Tris… radios', 'three rays', 'tris' Greenough's form of the accusative 'tres', with the noun understood after each later 'tris'. Each pair is a genitive singular: 'imbris torti', 'of twisted rain', i.e. hail, rain wrung tight into ice (so the ancient commentators explain it, from memory); 'nubis aquosae', 'of watery cloud'; 'rutili… ignis', 'of ruddy fire'; 'alitis austri', 'of the winged south wind'. Twelve rays in all, of hail, rain, fire and wind, the stuff of a storm. 'addiderant', pluperfect, 'had (already) added'. The Latin Library prints 'rutuli', which would make the fire 'Rutulian' and gives no sense here; Greenough's 'rutili', 'red', is the reading translated. No elisions.

sentences.t:
fulgores nunc horrificos sonitumque metumque
miscebant operi flammisque sequacibus iras.
sentences.l:
flashes now fearful and sound and fear
they were mixing into the work and with flames pursuing wraths.
sentences.i: now they were blending into the work the terrible flashes, the noise, the fear, and wrath with its pursuing flames.
sentences.n: 'nunc', 'now', at the moment Vulcan arrives: the last ingredients are not matter but effects. 'fulgores… horrificos', 'dreadful flashes'; 'sonitumque metumque', 'both the sound and the fear', the double '-que'; 'iras', 'wraths', 'flammis… sequacibus', 'with pursuing flames', flames that chase what they strike. 'miscebant operi', 'were mixing into the work', 'operi' dative. The Latin Library prints 'terrificos', 'terrifying', for Greenough's 'horrificos'; the sense hardly changes. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Parte alia Marti currumque rotasque volucris
instabant, quibus ille viros, quibus excitat urbes;
sentences.l:
In a part other for Mars both a chariot and wheels winged
they were pressing on, with which he men, with which he rouses cities;
sentences.i: Elsewhere they were hurrying on a chariot for Mars, with its flying wheels, with which he stirs up men and stirs up cities;
sentences.n: 'Parte alia', 'in another part' of the workshop. 'Marti', dative, 'for Mars'. 'currumque rotasque', 'both a chariot and wheels', the double '-que', the wheels singled out for their speed: 'volucris', accusative plural in '-is', 'winged', 'flying'. 'instabant', 'were pressing on with', 'were busy on', here with a direct object. 'quibus… quibus', 'with which… with which', anaphora: 'ille', Mars, 'excitat', 'rouses', both 'viros' and 'urbes', the verb shared. Elision 'Part(e) alia'.

sentences.t:
aegidaque horriferam, turbatae Palladis arma,
certatim squamis serpentum auroque polibant
conexosque anguis ipsamque in pectore divae
Gorgona, desecto vertentem lumina collo.
sentences.l:
and the aegis bristling, of roused Pallas the arms,
vying with scales of serpents and with gold they were polishing,
and the intertwined snakes and herself on the breast of the goddess
the Gorgon, with severed rolling her eyes neck.
sentences.i: and they were vying with one another to burnish the dread aegis, the armour of Pallas when her anger is roused, with serpents' scales and gold, the knotted snakes, and on the goddess's breast the Gorgon herself, rolling her eyes above her severed neck.
sentences.n: 'aegida', Greek accusative of 'aegis', the goatskin cloak or breastplate of Pallas Athena, fringed with snakes and bearing the Gorgon's head; Homer describes it with the Gorgon at its centre (Iliad 5, from memory). This Pallas is the goddess, not Evander's son, who appears at 466. 'horriferam', 'bristling'. 'turbatae Palladis arma', 'the arms of Pallas when roused', in apposition. 'certatim', 'in rivalry'. 'squamis serpentum auroque', 'with scales of serpents and with gold', ablatives of material. 'polibant', the old form of the imperfect, = 'poliebant', 'they were polishing'. 'conexos… anguis', 'the intertwined snakes', accusative plural in '-is'. 'ipsam… Gorgona', 'the Gorgon herself', 'Gorgona' Greek accusative, the head of Medusa cut off by Perseus; 'desecto… collo', ablative absolute, 'her neck severed', framing 'vertentem lumina', 'rolling her eyes', still alive in the metal. Elisions 'aegidaqu(e) horriferam', 'serpent(um) auroque', 'conexosqu(e) anguis', 'ipsamqu(e) in'.

sentences.t:
“Tollite cuncta, inquit, coeptosque auferte labores,
Aetnaei Cyclopes, et huc advertite mentem:
sentences.l:
“Take away everything,” he says, “and the begun carry off tasks,
Aetnaean Cyclopes, and here turn your mind:
sentences.i: “Put everything away,” he said, “and carry off the work you have begun, Cyclopes of Etna, and turn your minds to this:
sentences.n: Vulcan's speech opens here and runs to 443. 'Tollite cuncta', 'remove everything', the plural imperative to the whole crew. 'inquit', 'he says', interrupting the speech: Greenough prints it with commas and without closing and reopening the marks, his habit (as 8.351); l and i supply them. 'coeptos… labores', 'the tasks begun', framing 'auferte', 'take away'. 'Aetnaei Cyclopes', vocative, 'Cyclopes of Etna', their usual home; 'Cy-clō-pĕs', the Greek plural '-es' short. 'huc advertite mentem', 'turn your mind hither', the singular 'mentem' for the attention of all. Elisions 'cunct(a) inquit', 'coeptosqu(e) auferte'.

sentences.t: arma acri facienda viro.
sentences.l: arms for a fierce must be made man.
sentences.i: arms must be made for a fierce warrior.
sentences.n: 'arma… facienda (sunt)', 'arms are to be made', the gerundive of obligation with 'sunt' left out. 'acri… viro', 'for a fierce man', dative, framing 'facienda'. Vulcan does not name him: Aeneas, as at the start of the poem, is 'the man' ('virum', 1.1), and 'arma' and 'viro' stand in the line together. Elision 'arm(a) acri'.

sentences.t:
Nunc viribus usus,
nunc manibus rapidis, omni nunc arte magistra.
sentences.l:
Now of strength there is need,
now of hands swift, now of all masterly art.
sentences.i: Now there is need of strength, now of quick hands, now of all your mastery of the craft.
sentences.n: 'usus (est)', 'there is need', with the ablative 'viribus', 'of strength', and then of 'manibus rapidis', 'swift hands', and 'omni… arte magistra', 'all your master craft', 'magistra' used as an adjective, 'art as a teacher', 'master skill'. 'nunc… nunc… nunc', anaphora, the orders rapping out. No elisions.

sentences.t: Praecipitate moras. ”Nec plura effatus;
sentences.l: Hurl headlong delays.” No more having spoken;
sentences.i: Make haste, no delay!” He said no more;
sentences.n: The print has 'moras. ”Nec', with a space before the closing mark and none after it, a misprint for 'moras.” Nec', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. Because the mark is joined to 'Nec', this unit also carries 'Nec plura effatus', as at 8.404. 'Praecipitate moras', 'throw delays headlong', a vivid way of saying 'make haste'. Vulcan's speech ends. 'Nec plura effatus (est)', 'and he spoke no more', from the deponent 'effor'. Elision 'plur(a) effatus'.

sentences.t:
at illi
ocius incubuere omnes pariterque laborem
sortiti.
sentences.l:
but they
more swiftly bent to it all, and equally the labour
shared by lot.
sentences.i: and they all fell to the work at once, sharing out the labour equally by lot.
sentences.n: 'at illi', 'but they', the Cyclopes. 'ocius', 'quicker', comparative adverb, 'at once', 'with all speed'. 'incubuere' = 'incubuerunt', 'they bent to it', 'leaned on', the '-ere' perfect (you know it by now). 'pariter… sortiti (sunt)', 'they shared out by lot equally', 'sortior', deponent, 'to cast lots for', with 'laborem' as object. Elision 'incubuer(e) omnes'.

sentences.t:
Fluit aes rivis aurique metallum,
volnificusque chalybs vasta fornace liquescit.
sentences.l:
Flows bronze in streams and of gold the metal,
and wound-making steel in the vast furnace melts.
sentences.i: Bronze flows in streams, and gold, and the steel that deals wounds melts in the huge furnace.
sentences.n: 'Fluit aes rivis', 'bronze flows in streams', 'rivis' ablative of manner. 'auri… metallum', 'the metal of gold', just 'gold'. 'volnificus', Greenough's spelling of 'vulnificus' ('volnus' for 'vulnus' again), 'wound-making', a compound in the old epic manner. 'chalybs', 'steel', from the Chalybes (421). 'liquescit', 'grows liquid', an inceptive verb. Bronze, gold and steel: in Iliad 18 Hephaestus throws bronze, tin, gold and silver into the fire for Achilles' armour (from memory). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ingentum clipeum informant, unum omnia contra
tela Latinorum, septenosque orbibus orbes
impediunt.
sentences.l:
Huge a shield they shape, one against all
the weapons of the Latins, and sevenfold with circles circles
they interlock.
sentences.i: They shape a huge shield, a match by itself for all the weapons of the Latins, and bind together seven layers of circles, one upon another.
sentences.n: The print has 'Ingentum', a misprint for 'Ingentem', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. No Latin word 'ingentum' agrees with 'clipeum': the accusative of 'ingens' is 'ingentem', which the Latin Library prints and the metre allows equally. 'clipeum informant', 'they shape a shield', the shield whose pictures will close the book. 'unum omnia contra tela Latinorum', 'one against all the weapons of the Latins', 'unum' and 'omnia' set side by side, 'contra' between 'omnia' and its noun 'tela'. 'septenosque orbibus orbes impediunt', 'and they interlock sevenfold circles with circles', seven layers of metal plate fastened one over another, 'orbibus orbes' a striking repetition. The sevenfold shield is Ajax's in Homer (Iliad 7, from memory); Achilles' new shield has five layers (Iliad 18 and 20). Elisions 'clipe(um) informant', 'un(um) omnia', 'septenosqu(e) orbibus'.

sentences.t:
Alii ventosis follibus auras
accipiunt redduntque, alii stridentia tingunt
aera lacu.
sentences.l:
Others with windy bellows the airs
take in and give back, others hissing dip
bronzes in the trough.
sentences.i: Some take in the air and send it out again with bellows full of wind; others dip the hissing bronze into the water-trough.
sentences.n: 'Alii… alii', 'some… others'. 'ventosis follibus', 'with windy bellows', ablative of means; 'auras accipiunt redduntque', 'take in and give back the breezes', the bellows filling and emptying. Hephaestus works twenty bellows at once in Iliad 18 (from memory). 'stridentia… aera', 'hissing bronzes', 'aera' neuter plural of 'aes', the hot metal hissing as it is quenched; 'tingunt… lacu', 'dip in the trough', 'lacus' here a vat of water. Elision 'redduntqu(e) alii'.

sentences.t: Gemit impositis incudibus antrum.
sentences.l: Groans with the set-on anvils the cave.
sentences.i: The cave groans under the weight of the anvils set upon it.
sentences.n: 'Gemit… antrum', 'the cave groans', verb first and subject last, framing the line's second half. 'impositis incudibus', 'with the anvils set upon it', ablative of cause: the cave's floor groans under the anvils and the blows. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Illi inter sese multa vi bracchia tollunt
in numerum versantque tenaci forcipe massam.
sentences.l:
They among themselves with much force their arms raise
into rhythm, and turn with gripping tongs the mass.
sentences.i: They raise their arms with mighty force, one after another, in time, and turn the glowing lump with the gripping tongs.
sentences.n: 'Illi', 'they', the Cyclopes at the anvils. 'inter sese', 'among themselves', 'by turns'. 'multa vi', 'with much force'. 'bracchia tollunt in numerum', 'raise their arms in rhythm', 'numerus' the beat: the hammer-blows fall in time. 'tenaci forcipe', 'with gripping tongs', framing 'versant… massam', 'turn the mass' of metal on the anvil. Virgil had used nearly the same two lines of the Cyclopes in a simile for bees in the Georgics (Book 4, from memory). Elision 'Ill(i) inter'.

sentences.t:
Haec pater Aeoliis properat dum Lemnius oris,
Euandrum ex humili tecto lux suscitat alma
et matutini volucrum sub culmine cantus.
sentences.l:
These things while the father on the Aeolian hastens, the Lemnian, shores,
Evander from his humble roof the light rouses, kindly,
and of morning the birds' under the eaves songs.
sentences.i: While the Lemnian father was pressing on with this work on the Aeolian shores, the kindly light of day and the morning songs of the birds under the eaves roused Evander in his humble house.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough: the scene moves back to Pallanteum. 'Haec… properat dum', 'while (he) hastens these things', 'dum' postponed to fifth place; 'properare' with an object, 'to hurry on' a task. 'pater… Lemnius', 'the Lemnian father', Vulcan, from Lemnos, where Hephaestus fell when Zeus threw him out of heaven (Iliad 1, from memory), and where he was worshipped. 'Aeoliis… oris', 'on the Aeolian shores', enclosing 'properat dum Lemnius'. 'Euandrum… lux suscitat alma', 'the nurturing light rouses Evander'; 'Eu-' is one syllable. 'ex humili tecto', 'from his lowly roof', the humble house of 8.359–368. 'matutini volucrum sub culmine cantus', 'the morning songs of birds under the roof-ridge', 'matutini… cantus' framing 'volucrum sub culmine'. Elision 'Euandr(um) ex'.

sentences.t:
Consurgit senior tunicaque inducitur artus
et Tyrrhena pedum circumdat vincula plantis;
sentences.l:
Rises the old man and with a tunic draws on his limbs,
and Tyrrhenian of his feet he puts round bonds the soles;
sentences.i: The old man rose, put his tunic on over his limbs and tied Etruscan sandals round the soles of his feet;
sentences.n: 'Consurgit senior', 'the old man rises', 'senior' as often for 'old man', not a comparison. 'tunica… inducitur artus', 'he is drawn on as to his limbs with a tunic', i.e. 'he puts a tunic on his limbs', the passive used like the Greek middle voice with an accusative ('artus') of the part concerned; you have seen this with 'nudus membra' (425). 'Tyrrhena… vincula', 'Tyrrhenian bonds', the straps of Etruscan sandals; Etruscan sandals were a known fashion. 'pedum… plantis', 'the soles of his feet', dative with 'circumdat', 'puts round'. Elision 'tunicaqu(e) inducitur'.

sentences.t:
tum lateri atque umeris Tegeaeum subligat ensem,
demissa ab laeva pantherae terga retorquens.
sentences.l:
then to his side and shoulders a Tegean he fastens sword,
hanging down from the left a panther's hide throwing back.
sentences.i: then he buckled his Tegean sword to his side, with its strap over his shoulder, and threw back the panther-skin that hung down on his left.
sentences.n: 'tum', 'then', the dressing done in order, like a Homeric hero's arming. 'lateri atque umeris', 'to his side and shoulders', datives with 'subligat', 'fastens beneath', the sword hanging at the side from a baldric over the shoulder. 'Tegeaeum… ensem', 'a Tegean sword', from Tegea in Arcadia, Evander's homeland. 'demissa ab laeva', 'hanging down from the left', with 'pantherae terga', 'the panther's hide', poetic plural 'terga', 'backs', for the skin; 'retorquens', 'twisting back', throwing it back over his shoulder. Elisions 'later(i) atque', 'atqu(e) umeris', 'demiss(a) ab'.

sentences.t:
Nec non et gemini custodes limine ab alto
praecedunt gressumque canes comitantur erilem.
sentences.l:
Nor not also twin guardians from the threshold high
go before and the step dogs accompany of their master.
sentences.i: Two watchdogs too went before him from the high threshold and kept pace with their master's steps.
sentences.n: 'Nec non et', 'and also', 'and besides', a double negative making a positive. 'gemini custodes… canes', 'twin guardians… dogs', the noun held back to the second line. 'limine ab alto', 'from the high threshold', the preposition between noun and adjective. 'gressum… erilem', 'the master's step', framing 'canes comitantur'; 'erilis' is 'herilis', from 'erus' ('herus'), 'master'. Telemachus goes to the assembly with two dogs at his side (Odyssey 2, from memory): the homely detail is Homeric. Elision 'limin(e) ab'.

sentences.t:
Hospitis Aeneae sedem et secreta petebat
sermonum memor et promissi muneris heros.
sentences.l:
Of his guest Aeneas the abode and the private part he was seeking,
of their talk mindful and of the promised gift, the hero.
sentences.i: The hero was making for the lodging and private quarters of his guest Aeneas, mindful of their talk and of the help he had promised.
sentences.n: 'Hospitis Aeneae', 'of his guest Aeneas', genitive with both 'sedem' and 'secreta', 'the dwelling and the private part' of the house where Aeneas slept. 'petebat', imperfect, 'was making for'. 'sermonum memor', 'mindful of their conversations', and 'promissi muneris', 'of the promised gift', the help Evander promised at their first meeting (8.169–171). 'heros', 'the hero', held to the end: Evander. Elision 'sed(em) et'.

sentences.t: Nec minus Aeneas se matutinus agebat.
sentences.l: No less Aeneas, in the morning, was bestirring himself.
sentences.i: No less early was Aeneas astir.
sentences.n: 'Nec minus', 'no less', litotes. 'se… agebat', 'was moving himself', 'was on the move'. 'matutinus', 'in the morning', an adjective where English uses an adverb, common in Latin with words of time. No elisions.

sentences.t: Filius huic Pallas, illi comes ibat Achates.
sentences.l: Son to this one Pallas, to that one companion went Achates.
sentences.i: With the king went his son Pallas, with Aeneas his comrade Achates.
sentences.n: 'Filius huic Pallas, illi comes ibat Achates', 'his son Pallas (went) with this one, Achates as companion with that one', 'ibat' shared by both halves, the two clauses balanced. 'huic' and 'illi' are datives of reference, and by sense 'huic' is Evander (Pallas is his son) and 'illi' Aeneas, against the usual rule that 'hic' means the nearer, latter name. 'Achates', Aeneas's faithful companion since Book I. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Congressi iungunt dextras mediisque residunt
aedibus et licito tandem sermone fruuntur.
sentences.l:
Having met they join right hands and in the middle sit down
of the house, and permitted at last talk enjoy.
sentences.i: They met and clasped right hands, sat down in the middle of the house, and at last enjoyed the free talk now allowed them.
sentences.n: 'Congressi', 'having met', perfect participle of the deponent 'congredior'. 'iungunt dextras', 'they join right hands', the gesture of friendship and good faith. 'mediis… aedibus', 'in the middle of the house', the hall or courtyard, framing 'residunt'. 'licito… sermone', 'permitted talk', ablative with 'fruuntur', 'enjoy' ('fruor' takes the ablative): talk now free, the day before having been taken up with the feast and the rites of Hercules. No elisions.

sentences.t: Rex prior haec:
sentences.l: The king first these words:
sentences.i: The king spoke first:
sentences.n: A half-line, one of those Virgil left unfinished in the unrevised poem. 'Rex prior', 'the king first', 'haec', 'these things', with the verb of speaking left out ('Aeolus haec contra'). No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Maxume Teucrorum ductor, quo sospite numquam
res equidem Troiae victas aut regna fatebor,
nobis ad belli auxilium pro nomine tanto
exiguae vires:
sentences.l:
“Greatest of the Teucrians leader, whom being safe never
the power indeed of Troy conquered or its realms will I confess,
to us for of war help in respect of a name so great
slight is the strength:
sentences.i: “Greatest leader of the Teucrians — for while you live I will never admit that Troy's power or kingdom is overthrown — we have little strength to help you in war, little for a name so great:
sentences.n: Evander's speech opens here and runs to the end of this part. 'Maxume', vocative of 'maxumus', Greenough's old spelling of 'maxime' ('maxumus' for 'maximus' again). 'Teucrorum ductor', 'leader of the Teucrians'; 'Teu-' is one syllable. 'quo sospite', ablative absolute, 'you being safe', 'while you survive'. 'res… Troiae victas aut regna fatebor', 'I will admit that Troy's state or realms are conquered', 'victas' agreeing with 'res' and understood with 'regna'. 'equidem', 'I for my part'. 'nobis… exiguae vires (sunt)', 'to us is slight strength', a dative of possession, 'we have little strength'. 'ad belli auxilium', 'for help in war'. 'pro nomine tanto', 'in proportion to so great a name', Aeneas's fame. Elision 'bell(i) auxilium'.

sentences.t:
hinc Tusco claudimur amni,
hinc Rutulus premit et murum circumsonat armis.
sentences.l:
on this side by the Tuscan we are shut in river,
on that the Rutulian presses and the wall makes ring round with arms.
sentences.i: on one side the Tuscan river hems us in, on the other the Rutulian presses hard and rings our walls with the clash of arms.
sentences.n: 'hinc… hinc', 'on this side… on that', anaphora. 'Tusco… amni', 'by the Tuscan river', the Tiber, the boundary of Etruria, framing 'claudimur'. 'Rutulus', 'the Rutulian', collective singular for Turnus's people. 'murum circumsonat armis', 'makes the wall resound all round with arms'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Sed tibi ego ingentis populos opulentaque regnis
iungere castra paro, quam fors inopina salutem
ostentat:
sentences.l:
But to you I huge peoples and rich in kingdoms
to join a camp am preparing, which unlooked-for chance as a deliverance
holds out:
sentences.i: But I am preparing to join to you mighty peoples and an army rich in kingdoms, a deliverance which a chance no one foresaw now holds out:
sentences.n: 'Sed tibi ego', 'but to you I', the pronouns side by side. 'ingentis populos', 'huge peoples', accusative plural in '-is'. 'opulenta… regnis… castra', 'a camp rich in kingdoms', the Etruscan army drawn from many cities, 'regnis' ablative with an adjective of plenty. 'iungere… paro', 'I am preparing to join'. 'quam fors inopina salutem ostentat', 'which salvation unexpected chance shows', the antecedent drawn into the relative clause: 'a salvation which chance holds out'. Elisions 'tib(i) ego', 'eg(o) ingentis'.

sentences.t: fatis huc te poscentibus adfers.
sentences.l: with the fates here you demanding you bring yourself.
sentences.i: you come here at the call of the fates.
sentences.n: 'fatis… poscentibus', ablative absolute, 'the fates demanding (you)', framing 'huc te'. 'adfers', 'you bring yourself', with 'te', 'you come'; 'adfero' is Greenough's unassimilated spelling of 'affero'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Haud procul hinc saxo incolitur fundata vetusto
urbis Agyllinae sedes, ubi Lydia quondam
gens, bello praeclara, iugis insedit Etruscis.
sentences.l:
Not far from here, on rock is inhabited, founded ancient,
of the city Agyllan the seat, where the Lydian once
race, in war renowned, on the ridges settled Etruscan.
sentences.i: Not far from here, founded on ancient rock, stands the city of Agylla, where long ago a Lydian people famous in war settled on the Etruscan hills.
sentences.n: 'Haud procul hinc', 'not far from here'. 'saxo… fundata vetusto', 'founded on ancient rock', framing 'incolitur', 'is inhabited'. 'urbis Agyllinae sedes', 'the seat of the Agyllan city', the genitive of definition: the city itself. Agylla is the Greek name of Caere (Cerveteri), north-west of Rome. 'Lydia… gens', 'the Lydian race', split across the line-end: the ancients held that the Etruscans came from Lydia in Asia Minor (Herodotus, Book 1, from memory). 'bello praeclara', 'famous in war'. 'iugis… Etruscis', 'on the Etruscan hills', framing 'insedit', 'settled'. Elision 'sax(o) incolitur'.

sentences.t:
Hanc multos florentem annos rex deinde superbo
imperio et saevis tenuit Mezentius armis.
sentences.l:
This, many flourishing years, a king afterwards with proud
rule and with savage held, Mezentius, arms.
sentences.i: It had flourished for many years when King Mezentius took hold of it with arrogant rule and savage arms.
sentences.n: 'Hanc', the city, 'multos florentem annos', 'flourishing for many years', accusative of duration. 'rex deinde', 'a king afterwards', with the name held back: 'Mezentius', 'the despiser of the gods' of the catalogue (7.648). 'deinde', two syllables here, 'dein-de'. 'superbo imperio et saevis… armis', 'with proud rule and savage arms', 'superbo imperio' framing the line-break, 'saevis… armis' framing 'tenuit Mezentius'. 'superbus' is the word Romans used of tyrants: Tarquinius Superbus. Elisions 'florent(em) annos', 'imperi(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Quid memorem infandas caedes, quid facta tyranni
effera?
sentences.l:
Why should I recall the unspeakable slaughters, why the deeds of the tyrant
savage?
sentences.i: Why should I tell of his unspeakable murders, or the brutal acts of the tyrant?
sentences.n: 'Quid memorem', 'why should I recount', the deliberative subjunctive, introducing the device of passing over what one then tells (praeteritio). 'infandas caedes', 'unspeakable slaughters'. 'facta tyranni effera', 'the savage deeds of the tyrant', 'effera' held to the next line for weight. Elision 'memor(em) infandas'.

sentences.t: Di capiti ipsius generique reservent!
sentences.l: May the gods for the head of himself and for his race keep them in store!
sentences.i: May the gods keep the like in store for his own head and his children's!
sentences.n: 'Di', 'gods', = 'dei'. 'reservent', subjunctive of wish, 'may they keep in store', with the object understood: the same horrors. 'capiti ipsius', 'for his own head', the head standing for the person, a form of curse; 'generi', 'for his race', his line, his son Lausus (7.649–654). 'ipsius' has three syllables, ip-sī-us. Elision 'capit(i) ipsius'.

sentences.t:
Mortua quin etiam iungebat corpora vivis
componens manibusque manus atque oribus ora,
tormenti genus, et sanie taboque fluentis
complexu in misero longa sic morte necabat.
sentences.l:
Dead nay even he used to join bodies to living men,
setting together both hands to hands and mouths to mouths,
a kind of torture, and with gore and with corruption flowing,
in an embrace wretched, thus by a long death he killed.
sentences.i: He would even bind the dead to the living, fitting hands to hands and mouths to mouths, a form of torture, and so, as they oozed with gore and corruption in that horrible embrace, he would kill them by a slow death.
sentences.n: 'quin etiam', 'nay even', going a step further. 'Mortua… corpora', 'dead bodies', framing 'quin etiam iungebat', and 'vivis', 'to the living'; 'iungebat', iterative imperfect, 'used to join'. 'componens', 'setting together'. 'manibusque manus atque oribus ora', 'hands to hands and mouths to mouths', datives and accusatives side by side, limb fitted to limb. 'tormenti genus', 'a kind of torture', in apposition to the whole act. 'sanie taboque fluentis', 'flowing with gore and corruption', 'fluentis' accusative plural agreeing with the victims understood; 'sanies' is the bloody matter of wounds, 'tabum' the fluid of decay. 'complexu in misero', 'in the wretched embrace'. 'longa… morte', 'by a long death'. Cicero, in a lost work quoted by Augustine, likened the soul bound to the body to the captives Etruscan pirates killed this way (from memory). Elisions 'atqu(e) oribus', 'complex(u) in'.

sentences.t:
at fessi tandem cives infanda furentem
armati circumsistunt ipsumque domumque,
obtruncant socios, ignem ad fastigia iactant.
sentences.l:
But wearied at last the citizens, him raging unspeakable things,
in arms surround, both himself and his house,
cut down his followers, fire to the roof-tops hurl.
sentences.i: But at last the citizens could bear no more; they took up arms and surrounded him in his monstrous frenzy, himself and his house, cut down his followers and hurled fire on to the roof.
sentences.n: The print has 'at', lowercase after the full stop that ends 488, a misprint for 'At', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'fessi tandem cives', 'the citizens, weary at last'. 'infanda furentem', 'raging unspeakable things', an internal accusative with 'furo'. 'armati', 'armed', 'circumsistunt', 'surround'. 'ipsumque domumque', 'both himself and his house', the double '-que'. 'obtruncant socios', 'they butcher his followers', his guards. 'ignem ad fastigia iactant', 'they throw fire to the gables'. The historic presents quicken the pace. Elision 'ign(em) ad'.

sentences.t:
Ille inter caedem Rutulorum elapsus in agros
confugere et Turni defendier hospitis armis.
sentences.l:
He amid the slaughter into the Rutulians' having slipped out fields
fled for refuge, and of Turnus was defended, his host, by the arms.
sentences.i: In the midst of the slaughter he slipped away and fled for refuge to the land of the Rutulians, where the arms of his friend Turnus protect him.
sentences.n: 'Ille', Mezentius. 'inter caedem', 'amid the slaughter'. 'Rutulorum… in agros', 'into the fields of the Rutulians', framing 'elapsus', 'having slipped away'. 'confugere' and 'defendier' are historic infinitives, used like a past indicative in lively narrative: 'he fled and was protected'. 'defendier' is the old present passive infinitive in '-ier', = 'defendi', an archaism Virgil keeps for weight. 'Turni… hospitis armis', 'by the arms of Turnus his host', ablative of means; 'hospes' is a guest-friend, the bond of hospitality. Elisions 'Ill(e) inter', 'Rutulor(um) elapsus', 'confuger(e) et'.

sentences.t: Ergo omnis furiis surrexit Etruria iustis:
sentences.l: Therefore all in furies rose up Etruria righteous:
sentences.i: So all Etruria has risen in just rage:
sentences.n: 'Ergo', 'therefore'. 'omnis… Etruria', 'all Etruria', framing the verb. 'furiis… iustis', 'with just furies', enclosing 'surrexit Etruria': 'furiae' is usually madness, here a fury the speaker calls just. 'surrexit', 'has risen'. Elision 'Erg(o) omnis'.

sentences.t: regem ad supplicium praesenti Marte reposcunt.
sentences.l: the king to punishment with present Mars they demand back.
sentences.i: they demand the king back for punishment, with war on the spot.
sentences.n: 'regem ad supplicium… reposcunt', 'they demand the king back for punishment', from Turnus, who shelters him. 'praesenti Marte', 'with Mars at hand', 'with instant war', ablative of manner; Mars for war, as often (metonymy). Elision 'reg(em) ad'.

sentences.t: his ego te, Aenea, ductorem milibus addam.
sentences.l: To these I you, Aeneas, as leader thousands will add.
sentences.i: To these thousands I shall give you, Aeneas, as their leader.
sentences.n: The print has 'his', lowercase after the full stop that ends 495, a misprint for 'His', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'his… milibus', 'to these thousands', dative with 'addam', framing the line. 'te… ductorem', 'you as leader', predicative. 'Aenea', vocative of 'Aeneas', the Greek form. Elision 't(e) Aenea'.

sentences.t:
Toto namque fremunt condensae litore puppes
Signaque ferre iubent;
sentences.l:
For all along the shore roar, packed close, the ships,
and the standards to carry forward they bid;
sentences.i: For along the whole shore their ships lie packed close together and roar with men who call for the standards to advance;
sentences.n: The print has 'Signaque', with a capital in mid-sentence (497 ends with no stop), a misprint for 'signaque', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. 'namque', 'for', giving the reason for 'his milibus'. 'Toto… litore', 'along the whole shore', framing 'fremunt condensae', 'roar, crowded close'; 'puppes', 'sterns', for the ships, and the ships for the men aboard. 'signa ferre iubent', 'they bid carry the standards', the military order to advance. No elisions.

sentences.t:
retinet longaevus haruspex
“fata canens, O Maeoniae delecta iuventus,
flos veterum virtusque virum, quos iustus in hostem
fert dolor et merita accendit Mezentius ira,
nulli fas Italo tantam subiungere gentem:
sentences.l:
holds them back an aged soothsayer,
fates chanting: ‘O of Maeonia chosen youth,
flower of the old and valour of men, whom a just against the foe
carries resentment, and with deserved kindles Mezentius wrath,
for no Italian is it right so great to subdue a race:
sentences.i: but an aged soothsayer holds them back, chanting the decrees of fate: ‘Chosen warriors of Maeonia, the flower and valour of an ancient people, carried against the enemy by just resentment and set ablaze by Mezentius with a wrath he has earned, no man of Italy may master a nation so great:
sentences.n: The print has '“fata canens, O Maeoniae', the opening mark at the head of the line, a misprint for 'fata canens, “O Maeoniae': the soothsayer's words begin at 'O' (as 6.46, 6.52, 7.121); t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. Inside Evander's speech l and i give the prophecy in single marks, closed at 'duces' (503), where Greenough prints no mark. 'retinet', 'holds (them) back'. 'longaevus haruspex', 'an aged soothsayer', an Etruscan reader of entrails. 'Maeoniae', 'of Maeonia', the old name of Lydia (480). 'flos veterum virtusque virum', 'the flower and valour of men of old', 'virum' = 'virorum'. 'iustus… dolor', 'just resentment', framing 'in hostem fert'. 'merita… ira', 'with merited wrath', framing 'accendit Mezentius'. 'nulli fas Italo', 'it is right for no Italian', dative. 'subiungere', 'to bring under the yoke', 'sub-iun-ge-re'. Elision 'merit(a) accendit'.

sentences.t: externos optate duces;
sentences.l: foreign choose leaders.’
sentences.i: choose foreigners to lead you.’
sentences.n: 'externos… duces', 'foreign leaders', framing 'optate', 'choose', the plural imperative. The oracle's words end here, and they point at Aeneas, the stranger whom Latinus's oracle also foretold (7.98, 'externi venient generi'). The print has no mark here; l and i close the soothsayer's words. No elisions.

sentences.t:
tum Etrusca resedit
hoc acies campo, monitis exterrita divom.
sentences.l:
then the Etruscan sat down
in this the line plain, by the warnings terrified of the gods.
sentences.i: Then the Etruscan army settled down on this plain, daunted by the warnings of the gods.
sentences.n: 'tum', 'then', after the prophecy. 'Etrusca… acies', 'the Etruscan battle-line', framing 'resedit hoc', 'sat down', 'came to rest', and 'hoc… campo', 'on this plain', near by. 'monitis exterrita divom', 'terrified by the warnings of the gods', 'divom' = 'divorum', Greenough's old genitive plural (as always). Elision 't(um) Etrusca'.

sentences.t:
Ipse oratores ad me regnique coronam
cum sceptro misit mandatque insignia Tarchon,
succedam castris Tyrrhenaque regna capessam.
sentences.l:
Himself envoys to me and of the kingdom the crown
with the sceptre sent, and entrusts the insignia, Tarchon,
that I should come up to the camp and the Tyrrhenian kingdom take up.
sentences.i: Tarchon himself has sent envoys to me with the crown and sceptre of the kingdom, and hands over to me the emblems of royalty, asking me to come to the camp and take up the throne of Etruria.
sentences.n: 'Ipse… Tarchon', 'Tarchon himself', framing 505–506; Tarchon, the Etruscan leader who will join Aeneas in Book X. 'oratores', 'envoys', 'spokesmen'. 'regni… coronam cum sceptro', 'the crown of the kingdom with the sceptre'. 'mandat… insignia', 'entrusts the insignia', with 'succedam… capessam', 'that I should approach… and take up', subjunctives depending on 'mandat' without 'ut', as often after verbs of ordering. 'succedam castris', 'that I should come to the camp', dative with a compound verb. 'Tyrrhena… regna', 'the Tyrrhenian kingdom', poetic plural. 'capessam', 'take in hand', a desiderative of 'capio'. Elisions 'Ips(e) oratores', 'mandatqu(e) insignia'.

sentences.t:
Sed mihi tarda gelu saeclisque effeta senectus
invidet imperium seraeque ad fortia vires.
sentences.l:
But for me slow with chill and with ages worn out old age
grudges the command, and too late for brave deeds my strength.
sentences.i: But old age, slow with the chill of years and worn out by long time, begrudges me the command, and my strength comes too late for deeds of courage.
sentences.n: 'Sed mihi… senectus invidet imperium', 'but old age grudges me the command', 'invideo' with a dative of the person and an accusative of the thing, a poetic construction. 'tarda gelu', 'slow with cold', the cold of old blood. 'saeclis… effeta', 'worn out by ages', 'effetus', 'exhausted', literally 'past bearing'. 'seraeque ad fortia vires', 'and strength too late for brave deeds', a second subject of 'invidet': his strength comes too late in life. Elisions 'saeclisqu(e) effeta', 'seraequ(e) ad'.

sentences.t:
natum exhortarer, ni mixtus matre Sabella
hinc partem patriae traheret.
sentences.l:
My son I would urge on, if not, mixed from a mother Sabine,
from here a part of his fatherland he drew.
sentences.i: I would urge my son to take it, were it not that his Sabine mother has mixed his blood, and he draws part of his descent from this land.
sentences.n: The print has 'natum', lowercase after the full stop that ends 509, a misprint for 'Natum', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'natum exhortarer', 'I would urge on my son', the imperfect subjunctive of a present unreal condition, with 'ni… traheret', 'if he did not draw'. 'mixtus matre Sabella', 'mixed by a Sabine mother', 'Sabellus' an Oscan people's name used for Sabine. 'hinc', 'from here', from Italy: being half Italian, Pallas is barred by the prophecy ('nulli fas Italo', 502). 'partem patriae', 'a part of his fatherland', his country of origin. Elision 'nat(um) exhortarer'.

sentences.t:
Tu, cuius et annis
et generi fatum indulgent, quem numina poscunt,
ingredere, o Teucrum atque Italum fortissime ductor.
sentences.l:
You, whose both years
and race fate favours, whom the divine powers demand,
step in, O of Teucrians and Italians bravest leader.
sentences.i: You, whose years and whose birth fate favours, whom the gods call for, take up the task, bravest leader of Trojans and Italians alike.
sentences.n: The print has 'indulgent', a plural verb with the singular subject 'fatum', a misprint for 'indulget', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. The Latin Library prints 'indulget', and the metre allows either. 'cuius et annis et generi', 'to whose years and to whose race', datives with 'indulget', 'is kind to', 'favours': Aeneas is young enough and foreign enough. 'quem numina poscunt', 'whom the gods demand', echoing 'fatis… poscentibus' (477). 'ingredere', imperative of the deponent 'ingredior', 'step in', 'take it on'. 'Teucrum atque Italum', genitives plural, 'of Teucrians and Italians', the old short forms; Aeneas will lead both. 'fortissime ductor', vocative, ringing back to 'Maxume… ductor' (470). 'Teu-' is one syllable. Elisions 'fat(um) indulgent', 'ingreder(e) o', 'Teucr(um) atque', 'atqu(e) Italum'.

sentences.t:
hunc tibi praeterea, spes et solacia nostri,
Pallanta adiungam;
sentences.l:
This one to you besides, the hope and comfort of us,
Pallas I will join;
sentences.i: Besides, I will join to you this boy, my hope and comfort, Pallas;
sentences.n: The print has 'hunc', lowercase after the full stop that ends 513, a misprint for 'Hunc', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'hunc… Pallanta', 'this (one)… Pallas', framing the clause, 'Pallanta' the Greek accusative. 'praeterea', 'besides'. 'spes et solacia nostri', 'the hope and comforts of us', in apposition, 'nostri' the genitive of 'nos' used for 'me', 'my'. 'adiungam', 'I will join', 'ad-iun-gam'. Evander's offer of his son is the gift whose cost Book XI will count. Elision 'Pallant(a) adiungam'.

sentences.t:
sub te tolerare magistro
militiam et grave Martis opus, tua cernere facta
adsuescat primis et te miretur ab annis.
sentences.l:
under you to bear as master
soldiering and the heavy of Mars work, your to behold deeds
let him grow used, from first, and you let him admire, years.
sentences.i: under you as his teacher let him grow used to soldiering and the heavy work of war, to watching what you do, and let him look up to you from his earliest years.
sentences.n: 'sub te… magistro', 'under you as master', 'magistro' in apposition to 'te', 'with you as his teacher'. 'adsuescat', 'let him grow used', jussive subjunctive, governing two infinitives: 'tolerare', 'to endure', with two objects, 'militiam', 'soldiering', and 'grave Martis opus', 'the heavy work of Mars', war; and 'tua cernere facta', 'to see your deeds'. 'et te miretur', 'and let him admire you', a second jussive. 'primis… ab annis', 'from his first years', framing the clause: he is still young. 'adsuescat' is Greenough's spelling of 'assuescat', with consonantal 'u', 'ad-sues-cat'. Elision 'militi(am) et'.

sentences.t:
Arcadas huic equites bis centum, robora pubis
lecta dabo totidemque suo tibi nomine Pallas.”
sentences.l:
Arcadian to him horsemen two hundred, the strength of our youth
chosen, I will give, and as many in his own to you name Pallas.”
sentences.i: To him I will give two hundred Arcadian horsemen, the chosen strength of our young men, and Pallas will give you as many more in his own name.”
sentences.n: 'Arcadas… equites', 'Arcadian horsemen', 'Arcadas' the Greek accusative plural, framing 'huic', 'to him'. 'bis centum', 'twice a hundred'. 'robora pubis lecta', 'chosen strengths of the youth', in apposition: 'robur', 'oak', then 'hardness', 'strength', here the best of the fighting men. 'dabo', 'I will give'. 'totidemque', 'and as many', with 'dabit' understood: 'Pallas (will give) you as many in his own name', a gift from the son as well as the father, four hundred in all. 'suo… nomine', framing 'tibi'. Evander's speech ends, and Greenough closes the mark; the scene goes on in the next part. No elisions.
